routes.description: Establish a historical core of Jesus' death, burial or empty tomb, and postmortem appearances, then show that bodily resurrection explains that core within an adequately supported theistic framework.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical premises are sufficiently supported, bodily resurrection accounts for them more adequately than the live natural alternatives, and objections concerning testimony, prior probability, and miracle attribution do not defeat the inference.

motionBridge.description: Connect the supported historical core and comparative explanation directly to the rational conclusion that Jesus bodily rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Establish Jesus' death and burial or empty tomb together with reported postmortem experiences sufficiently robust to require explanation.
Show that the appearance and resurrection traditions concern a transformed physical body rather than only an inward or immaterial experience.
Show that hallucination, removal, survival, fraud, legend, and combinations of such accounts do not explain the historical core as adequately.
Provide sufficient background warrant for divine action and connect that framework specifically to Jesus so resurrection is an admissible historical explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the early, eyewitness-linked, and mutually reinforcing character of the traditions used to establish the historical premises.
Use claimed anomalous or survival evidence to challenge strict naturalistic exclusion without treating that evidence itself as proof of resurrection.

routes.description: Show that the partisan and limited historical record does not distinguish bodily resurrection from visionary, removal, error-based, or presently unreconstructable alternatives under an appropriate standard for miracle attribution.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if indispensable historical or bodily premises remain uncertain, the evidence remains underdetermined by available alternatives, or justified background beliefs about supernatural agency are insufficient to make resurrection the warranted conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Connect unresolved historical and epistemic underdetermination directly to the conclusion that bodily resurrection is not established by the evidence.

centralBridges.description: Show that chronology, partisan sourcing, limited independent testimony, and textual ambiguity constrain the historical premises available for the resurrection inference.
Show that grief visions, hallucination, body removal, error, or combinations of ordinary possibilities can resist the resurrection inference without a complete reconstruction.
Challenge whether reported seeing, touching, and spiritual-body language establish an externally observable and coherent bodily resurrection.
Require independently justified beliefs about a supernatural agent, its nature, and its intentions before unexplained evidence may rationally be attributed to miracle.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Treat inability to reconstruct a distant event as a reason for a tentative conclusion rather than as affirmative support for resurrection.
Require appropriate repeatability or independent validation before anomalous perception reports alter the background case for supernatural survival.

sections.title: Historical Sources and Early Tradition
sections.rationale: The dating, provenance, independence, and eyewitness linkage of Pauline, creedal, Gospel, and non-Christian material determine the evidential foundation available to both burden routes.

sections.title: Death, Burial, and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: Actual death and the disposition of Jesus' body are indispensable to bodily resurrection, while the empty-tomb evidence and ordinary removal possibilities shape what requires explanation.

sections.title: Appearances and Psychological Alternatives
sections.rationale: The reported experiences of disciples, groups, Paul, and other converts form the principal experiential basis of the case and the principal ground for visionary or hallucination accounts.

sections.title: Nature of the Resurrection Body
sections.rationale: Contact narratives, sensory reports, eating accounts, and Pauline spiritual-body language bear directly on whether the traditions support bodily resurrection rather than an immaterial manifestation.

sections.title: Comparative Explanation and Burden of Reconstruction
sections.rationale: The motion turns partly on whether resurrection must outperform a complete natural reconstruction or whether unresolved ordinary possibilities are enough to leave the evidence underdetermined.

sections.title: Miracle Priors and Worldview Evidence
sections.rationale: Prior beliefs about God, divine intention, natural law, anomalous perception, and survival after death affect when historical evidence can rationally support a specifically miraculous conclusion.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: The historical core presented for explanation includes transformative appearance experiences by the disciples and the conversions of James and Paul.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Habermas to present his case, and this uninterrupted answer precedes the handoff to Flew.

response.rationale: This constructive move identifies the principal reported experiences and conversions that the proposed historical explanation must address.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It efficiently establishes a central evidential datum within the class of constructive moves.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable as a report about experiences believed to be appearances, not direct proof of resurrection.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The wording distinguishes the subjects' beliefs from the truth of the resurrection interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The listed conversions and experiences coherently constitute phenomena requiring explanation, with only the historical-support bridge compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt identifies James, Paul, and scholarly common ground, but does not document each report or its independence here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies a major part of the historical core, placing it near the top of central-tier contact.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents affirmative historical data without developing or evaluating a live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names disciples' experiences and the conversions of James and Paul as experiences understood by them as appearances.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Agreement on proposed facts does not overcome an evidential record marked by uncertain chronology, partisan documents, absent Gospel eyewitnesses, and limited independent testimony.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Flew by name, and Flew expressly responds to Habermas's facts before the moderator asks Gary for an answer.

components.text: Whether the proposed historical core rests on sufficiently reliable and independently supported source material.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the evidential foundation of the asserted historical core through chronology, partisanship, eyewitness limits, and independence concerns.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive evidential premise, although several distinct source criticisms remain briefly developed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source critique is clear, but the excerpt's reference to all evidence being document-based risks scope compression.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The stated limitations support caution, though uncertain dates alone carry less weight than the broader conclusion suggests.

charity.alternative: The listed appearances and conversions may still be accepted as a limited historical core despite partisan sources.
charity.decisiveQualification: Acceptance of a minimal report does not establish its independence, accuracy, or resurrection interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from record limitations to reduced confidence is coherent, though the relative effect of each limitation is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific limitations are identified, but representative documentation and comparison of the sources are not supplied in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central burden of undercutting the historical record and its evidential sufficiency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges agreement on facts while fairly insisting that agreement does not eliminate source-quality constraints.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly cites unknown chronology and a documentary evidential base; the locked proposition also identifies partisan and eyewitness limitations.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: The First Corinthians 15 tradition is early, was received and transmitted by Paul, and is linked through his Jerusalem visit to Peter and James.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests an example from Gary's preceding answer, and the sustained first-person exposition is followed by a direct question to Tony.

components.text: Whether any important resurrection tradition is early and linked closely enough to named witnesses to mitigate the record limitations.

response.rationale: The reply answers the proximity concern with the dating and transmission formula of First Corinthians 15 and a proposed Jerusalem link to Peter and James.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly addresses chronology and witness linkage, while leaving broader Gospel independence and partisan-source concerns unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly separates the letter's date, the received tradition, and the probable source of Paul's material.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrase most likely appropriately qualifies the inference that Paul received the material from Peter and James.

charity.alternative: Early transmission does not itself establish eyewitness accuracy or independence of every resurrection account.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument mitigates proximity concerns but does not by itself verify the appearances or all later narratives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The chain from technical transmission language and the Jerusalem visit to early witness linkage is coherent with a bounded implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It gives specific textual and chronological support, though the inference about where Paul received the formula remains debated and compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary bridge concerning source proximity and sits at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly answers one major source objection without expressly claiming that early transmission settles every reliability issue.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt dates First Corinthians, cites Paul's received-and-delivered formula, and argues that Peter and James were its likely Jerusalem sources.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The disciples' reported experiences are plausibly grief-related visions with no externally visible object rather than encounters with a bodily risen Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Tony for his naturalistic theory, and the answer ends before the moderator introduces a related publication.

components.text: Whether the reported disciple experiences require an external bodily object rather than an ordinary psychological explanation.

response.rationale: The reply directly supplies a grief-vision interpretation of the appearance experiences and expressly denies that an externally visible object was present.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive interpretation of the disciple experiences, but does not account here for James, Paul, groups, or varied circumstances.

precisionFindings.rationale: The grief-vision hypothesis is clear, but its extension from bereavement examples to all relevant disciples is only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The commonness analogy makes the hypothesis plausible, but the categorical absence of an object exceeds the support given.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy offers a usable alternative inference, but the bridge from ordinary bereavement visions to the full appearance set is material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on a general example of bereavement experience without specific evidence about these subjects or group reports.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central burden of preserving a natural explanation for a principal class of appearances.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move proposes an alternative but does not substantially examine the strongest bodily or multi-witness version of the opposing case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt analogizes the reports to common experiences of bereaved people seeming to see a deceased relative and denies an external object.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Conversion disorder and grief hallucinations do not jointly explain Paul and the disciples because the proposed conditions lack evidence and do not fit the varied groups, circumstances, and transformations.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Gary whether the proposed psychological explanations work, and Gary delivers a continuous rebuttal until Flew is invited to respond.

components.text: Whether grief visions plausibly fit the relevant subjects, groups, circumstances, and resulting transformations.
Whether there is affirmative historical evidence for the psychological conditions attributed to Paul and the disciples.

response.rationale: The rebuttal attacks both the factual basis and explanatory fit of the proposed disorders and hallucinations, especially for Paul and the varied appearance claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly engages the decisive fit and evidential premises and extends the comparison across multiple subjects and circumstances.

precisionFindings.rationale: The overall comparative claim is clear, though several psychological labels are rapidly combined without fully stable definitions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The mismatch evidence supports a strong objection, but describing the problem as decisive compresses uncertainty about heterogeneous psychological accounts.

charity.alternative: Different psychological mechanisms might explain Paul and the disciples without requiring one uniform diagnosis.
charity.decisiveQualification: Multiplying mechanisms remains possible, but each proposed mechanism still needs subject-specific evidence and explanatory fit.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The mismatch argument is coherent and comparative, with only a bounded assumption that the cited conditions are necessary for each alternative.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies subject-specific absences and varied circumstances, but detailed psychological sources and the full underlying data are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the indispensable central task of defeating principal psychological alternatives.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes distinct theories and subjects, although its rapid treatment does not fully develop the strongest multi-causal alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies evidence that Paul wanted conversion and argues that the proposed conditions do not apply uniformly to Paul and the disciples.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Against extensive historical ignorance and severely limited non-Christian evidence, the reasonable conclusion is a tentative natural interpretation rather than a publicly observable physical resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: A question characterizes the psychological account as hypothesis, after which Flew answers in his distinctive first-person skeptical voice until the moderator intervenes.

components.text: Whether rejecting specific psychological reconstructions is enough to establish a publicly observable physical resurrection.
Whether the reported experiences warrant an external, visible, and photographable body rather than a restrained interpretation.
Whether early tradition overcomes the large residual ignorance surrounding the event and its interpretation.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing demand for a complete natural mechanism with the narrower historical demand of whether the evidence warrants a physical public event amid substantial ignorance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe preserves the legitimate comparative issue and answers it, though it does not directly resolve the detailed evidence against psychological accounts.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is expressly tentative, and the contrast with a publicly observable physical body is clearly defined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move carefully limits its conclusion to what can reasonably be inferred against a background of acknowledged ignorance.

charity.alternative: The available evidence could cumulatively support physical resurrection even without complete historical information.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cumulative support still must distinguish a public bodily event from underdetermined interpretations of sparse reports.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently derives restraint from underdetermination and explicitly avoids treating ignorance as a complete positive natural history.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic conclusion fits the acknowledged record limits, although the scale of historical ignorance is asserted more than demonstrated here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly connects underdetermination to the motion-level conclusion that physical resurrection is not established.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reframe fairly preserves the pro side's evidential aim while challenging whether that evidence crosses the required inferential threshold.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt emphasizes enormous background ignorance and recommends only a tentative interpretation without postulating a universally visible physical body.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: The Thomas narrative does not establish bodily contact because it reports an invitation to touch and subsequent sight but does not clearly report that Thomas actually touched Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Tony whether he accepts the four facts, and Flew's answer about Thomas continues until Gary is expressly asked to respond.

components.text: Whether the appearance evidence establishes physical contact rather than merely reported seeing or an invitation to touch.
Whether an appearance report by itself supplies evidence of an externally tangible body.

response.rationale: The reply narrows the bodily-evidence question to the textual distinction between an invitation to touch and an explicit report that Thomas touched Jesus.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts bodily interpretation but only indirectly answers the broader psychological rebuttal selected as the legal primary target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The textual distinction between an invitation, sight, and completed touching is precise and explicitly limited to Thomas.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cautious phrase as far as I can see matches the bounded textual ambiguity being asserted.

charity.alternative: The invitation and Thomas's response may contextually imply that the encounter concerned a tangible wounded body.
charity.decisiveQualification: Contextual implication is weaker than an explicit narrative statement that Thomas actually made contact.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is tightly limited: an unfulfilled or unreported invitation cannot alone establish that physical contact occurred.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument rests on a specific textual observation, though the surrounding Johannine context is not fully compared in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially advances the central challenge to bodily interpretation, but concerns only one contact narrative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection accurately preserves the contextual bodily implication while identifying the narrower evidential omission in the narrative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that Thomas was invited to touch but that the account does not clearly say he put his hands into the wounds.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Johannine reports of seeing and touching, together with Luke's flesh-and-bones language and eating scene, support a tangible physical resurrection body rather than a ghostly manifestation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker answers Flew's complaint about sparse touch evidence by citing Johannine and Lucan material, followed immediately by Flew's skeptical rejoinder.

components.text: Whether the broader resurrection narratives report actual sensory and physical interaction despite ambiguity about Thomas's completed touch.
Whether the reports include tangible, shared bodily features inconsistent with a merely ghostly grief experience.
Whether the evidence supports a physical body visible and tangible to observers.

response.rationale: The reply answers the Thomas limitation by broadening the evidence to Johannine touching language and Luke's flesh, bones, touching, and eating reports.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly addresses the decisive bodily-evidence demand using multiple sensory features, though textual reliability remains outside this answer.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly identifies which reported sensory details support the limited claim of a literal physical body.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrase evidence seems to show properly presents an evidential inference rather than certainty from the narratives.

charity.alternative: Narrative reports of touching and eating may be theological or literary developments rather than independent observations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even if source reliability remains contested, the narrative content itself plainly depicts tangible embodiment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Seeing, touching, flesh-and-bones language, and eating jointly support embodiment, subject to the separate reliability of the reports.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific Johannine and Lucan details are supplied, but dating, independence, and historical verification of those details remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central bodily-character bridge with several distinct sensory indicators.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply establishes what the texts portray but gives limited attention to the stronger source-critical challenge to their historical force.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites hands touching, Luke's invitation to touch, denial of ghostliness, eating, and repeated seeing and touching.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Calling a body spiritual appears incoherent because an immaterial substance has no identifiable characteristics and is not genuinely a body.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly invites Flew to answer, and the ensuing first-person objection continues until the next moderator question.

components.text: Whether the claimed resurrection body is conceptually coherent when it is also characterized as spiritual or immaterial.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the coherence of the body's characterization, arguing that immateriality supplies no bodily characteristics despite sensory claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive conceptual issue, although it assumes spiritual means immaterial without first engaging Paul's possible specialized usage.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clear, but spiritual and immaterial are treated as equivalent without a defended terminological bridge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual worry is legitimate, but saying an immaterial substance is nothing goes beyond the argument supplied.

charity.alternative: Spiritual body may denote a transformed body empowered by spirit rather than an immaterial substance.
charity.decisiveQualification: If that specialized meaning is textually supported, the alleged contradiction between spiritual and bodily does not follow.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument is valid only under the contested equivalence of spiritual and immaterial, leaving a substantial equivocation at its center.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies a philosophical assertion about immaterial substance but no textual or conceptual defense of the key equivalence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally challenges bodily coherence, though its contact is narrower than the sensory evidence it answers.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection materially weakens the strongest Pauline interpretation by equating spiritual with immaterial before addressing transformed embodiment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt equates spiritual with immaterial and argues that an immaterial substance lacks characteristics and is not genuinely a body.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Paul's spiritual-body language denotes a transformed body rather than a disembodied spirit, as clarified by his description of bodily transformation in Philippians 3.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator's exchange ends with agreement, after which Habermas explicitly addresses Tony and interprets the Pauline passages in sequence.

components.text: Whether Paul's phrase spiritual body means an immaterial or wispy spirit and is therefore internally incoherent.
Whether Pauline language supports a transformed physical body rather than an entirely nonphysical manifestation.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the objection's key semantic premise as anachronistic and uses Philippians 3 as Pauline clarification that transformation is not disembodiment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the allegedly defective equivalence, supplies a defeating textual consequence, and offers a cross-text clarification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move defines spiritual body by contrast with disembodiment and identifies bodily transformation as the intended sense.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The interpretive conclusion is presented as the speaker's reading and supported by a specified Pauline comparison.

charity.alternative: Spiritual body could still indicate a mode of existence discontinuous with ordinary physical embodiment.
charity.decisiveQualification: Discontinuity does not entail immateriality when Paul's comparison expressly describes transformation of the body.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response directly defeats the equivocation by distinguishing modern usage from Pauline usage and supplying an interpretive control.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Philippians 3 provides specific comparative support, though the relevant wording and broader exegetical alternatives are only summarized.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central bodily-character bridge by resolving a major conceptual objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply handles the strongest semantic alternative and identifies the decisive distinction between transformation and loss of embodiment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects reading spiritual through modern assumptions and treats Philippians 3 as commentary describing bodily transformation rather than nonphysical spirit.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Whether belief in an alleged miracle is rational depends on antecedent beliefs, so the same resurrection reports need not rationally support a miracle for someone who initially suspects error.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Tony by name, and Flew answers in the first person by contrasting his own priors with those of Jews and Christians.

components.text: Whether coherent bodily language alone makes miracle belief rational independently of a person's justified antecedent beliefs.
Whether sensory reports rationally require a miraculous conclusion for an observer whose prior expectation favors error.
Whether appearance reports have the same rational force under materially different antecedent beliefs.

response.rationale: The reply justifies shifting from textual coherence alone to the epistemic question of how the reports update differing justified priors about miracles.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe preserves the issue of rational inference, though it does not directly dispute the Pauline semantic interpretation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional dependence on prior belief and the possibility of later persuasion are both expressly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim concerns dependence on priors, while the speaker explicitly allows sufficiently spectacular evidence to change them.

charity.alternative: Strong enough likelihood evidence can rationally overwhelm a low prior probability of resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move permits that outcome but insists that the evidential threshold varies with justified prior commitments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional epistemic argument is explicit, consistent, and avoids claiming that skeptical priors are permanently unrevisable.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reasoning is philosophically grounded and internally illustrated, but no method is supplied for determining which priors are justified.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central requirement for prior theological warrant before miracle attribution.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately incorporates the strongest convergence response by allowing persuasion while preserving the relevance of prior probability.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that rational response to an alleged miracle depends on prior beliefs and allows unusually spectacular evidence to persuade a skeptic.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Jesus' death by crucifixion is supported cumulatively by medical considerations, broad critical acceptance, non-Christian attestations, and Paul's early preaching.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Habermas for evidence of death and outside sources, and the answer identifies medical, scholarly, extrabiblical, and Pauline support.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies several independent categories of support for the indispensable premise that Jesus actually died by crucifixion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It strongly establishes a central historical premise using cumulative support, though individual attestations are only summarized.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is narrowly focused on death by crucifixion and clearly identifies the cumulative support categories.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Strong confidence fits the convergent medical, scholarly, non-Christian, and early Pauline support described.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple support streams coherently converge on the limited historical conclusion that crucifixion resulted in Jesus' death.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The span identifies several representative evidence classes and critical acceptance, though medical and extrabiblical details are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Actual death is indispensable to the central historical core and this move supplies direct, high-value support.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move constructs the death premise and does not meaningfully engage a live survival or misidentification alternative in this span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes medical evidence, critical scholarly agreement, extrabiblical sources, and strong acceptance of Jesus' crucifixion.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Early attestation, hostile acknowledgment, proclamation in Jerusalem, and women as culturally unlikely invented witnesses jointly support the empty tomb.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests evidence that the tomb was empty, and Habermas enumerates four reasons before explicitly asking Flew to respond to them.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents four cumulative considerations intended to establish the empty tomb as part of the historical core.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It offers several mutually reinforcing considerations, with some historical warrants and source relationships left compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is clearly cumulative and identifies the limited conclusion each consideration is intended to support.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The considerations are probative, but hostile acknowledgment and Jerusalem proclamation require more qualification than the presentation gives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative structure is coherent, though the Jerusalem and hostile-admission inferences each contain a material compressed warrant.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Four specific considerations are identified, but their independence, dating, and susceptibility to alternative explanations remain underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The empty tomb materially supplies the central historical core and determines what bodily explanations must address.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states an affirmative cumulative case without directly comparing the strongest source-critical or body-removal explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies women witnesses, early Pauline attestation, Jewish acknowledgment, and Jerusalem proclamation as cumulative empty-tomb evidence.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: Without independent witnesses, many ordinary removals of a body remain possible, and the distant historical episode cannot be reliably reconstructed from the available evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator identifies the question as Flew's and Flew answers in his characteristic first-person form before the moderator turns back to Gary.

components.text: Whether the asserted empty tomb distinguishes resurrection from ordinary removal given the absence of independent witnesses.
Whether uncertainty about disposition of the body undermines the independently supported premise that crucifixion caused death.
Whether appearance reports determine what happened to the body.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers the explanatory force of the empty tomb by preserving multiple ordinary removal possibilities and historical non-reconstructability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive empty-tomb inference but leaves the four individual cumulative considerations mostly unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The speaker clearly distinguishes possibility of ordinary removal from any claim to possess a complete removal theory.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that several removals remain possible fits the admitted inability to reconstruct a complete history.

charity.alternative: The cumulative empty-tomb considerations may make some ordinary removals historically less likely.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reduced likelihood does not eliminate underdetermination where no independent witness identifies how the body disappeared.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from absent independent observation and multiple possible removals to restraint is coherent without requiring a complete rival narrative.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The absence of independent witnesses and generic removal possibilities support underdetermination, but no concrete historically fitted alternative is developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central burden of preserving natural alternatives to the empty-tomb inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply does not deny the cited considerations outright and fairly limits its conclusion to unresolved ordinary possibilities.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that there are no independent witnesses, many possible ways to remove bodies, and insufficient evidence for reconstruction.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Naturalistic alternatives fail to explain the evidence as a unified whole and require multiplying separate accounts for Jesus' death, the disciples' appearances, Paul's experience, and the empty tomb.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Gary to survey naturalistic accounts, and Habermas proceeds through swoon, fraud, hallucination, legend, and combined explanations.

components.text: Whether merely possible body-removal accounts explain the evidence as well as a unified resurrection hypothesis.
Whether one hallucination account can explain both Paul and the disciples.
Whether restraint alone answers the comparative explanatory demand posed by the combined evidence.

response.rationale: The reply compares explanatory scope and argues that separate mechanisms are needed for death, distinct appearances, and the empty tomb.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly engages the principal alternatives and their combined explanatory burden, although simplicity is not fully weighed against prior probability.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim concerns comparative unification, and the distinct phenomena requiring separate accounts are clearly identified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Multiplication is a genuine explanatory cost, but it does not alone show that resurrection has superior total probability.

charity.alternative: A composite natural explanation may be less unified yet still more probable than a miraculous explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Lower unification is not decisive by itself; comparative judgment must also include fit and background probability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scope comparison is coherent, though it leaves an important bridge from theoretical multiplication to overall explanatory inferiority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It names the phenomena and required mechanisms, but offers limited case-specific evaluation of each rival and their joint probabilities.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central burden of defeating principal alternatives through comparative explanatory scope.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes combined theories but understates the strongest response that ordinary mechanisms may tolerate complexity without losing overall probability.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that separate hallucination accounts are needed for Paul and the disciples and another account for the empty tomb.

moves.speaker: Antony Flew
moves.proposition: A satisfactory complete naturalistic reconstruction may be unavailable, while hallucination can still explain much of the appearance evidence even though it leaves the empty tomb unexplained.
moves.attributionBasis: Flew interrupts the characterization of his position with a first-person clarification, and the moderator then immediately asks him a new question.

components.text: Whether the con side must provide one satisfactory complete naturalistic reconstruction before resurrection remains unestablished.
Whether hallucination explains the empty tomb evidence.
Whether hallucination can explain a substantial portion of the appearance evidence despite acknowledged residual gaps.

response.rationale: The reply expressly rejects the demand for a complete naturalistic history and states the defeating consequence: partial ordinary explanations can preserve underdetermination despite an unexplained tomb.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly diagnoses the burden error and candidly identifies both what hallucination covers and what it does not cover.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move precisely distinguishes inability to offer a complete account from the narrower explanatory reach claimed for hallucination.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The admission that hallucination leaves the empty tomb unexplained appropriately limits the asserted naturalistic conclusion.

charity.alternative: A unified resurrection account may explain more of the evidence than the admitted fragmentary alternatives.
charity.decisiveQualification: Greater scope does not establish warranted inference unless the miraculous account's priors and evidential reliability also compare favorably.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between defeating an inference and reconstructing every detail is explicit and resolves the principal burden challenge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The burden argument is strong, but the claim that hallucination covers much of the data is not independently supported in this short span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply connects the absence of a complete rival directly to motion-level historical underdetermination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately concedes the pro account's scope advantage while denying that a complete rival is a prerequisite for restraint.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly declines a complete naturalistic reconstruction, claims hallucination covers much appearance data, and concedes the empty tomb remains uncovered.

moves.speaker: Gary Habermas
moves.proposition: Evidence for God, present-day anomalies, and survival after death can alter the relevant background assumptions and raise the prior plausibility of resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly invites Habermas to answer, and Flew's response begins immediately after this sustained turn.

components.text: Whether there is independent background evidence capable of raising the prior plausibility of resurrection.
Whether anomalous and survival evidence supplies a comparative answer to incomplete natural alternatives.
